fable-5.1.text:
I think there's something interesting going on right now, which is that it feels like both at the same time. If you look at the models, they're doing these amazing things, the evals are getting saturated, and yet when you look at the economy, at the day-to-day life of a person, it's... it's less than you would expect. The impact is lagging the capability, or at least the apparent capability.

And I think part of the reason is that the models are jagged. They're very good at some things and surprisingly bad at others, and they don't really learn on the job the way a person does. So you can't just hand them a job and walk away. A human employee makes mistakes, but then they notice and they fix it and they don't make it again. The models mostly don't do that yet. And so people try them, they're impressed, and then they go back to doing things more or less the way they did before.

But I think this is a property of this particular moment and not a property of the future. When the AI actually works, when it is reliable, when it can learn continually and do the things that a person can do, I don't think it will be subtle. I think it will be very felt. The economy will start to grow at a rate that's hard to imagine right now. There will be a lot more AI in the world, eventually in the physical world, and governments and companies will respond to it because they won't have a choice. The thing where you can read the news and think "well, not much has changed" — I think that will go away.

There is also a buffer, which is that the world moves slower than the technology. Adoption takes time, deployment takes time, people take time. That buffer is part of why it feels like little has changed. But at some point the buffer gets overwhelmed.

Now, there is one sense in which you might be right, which is that people adapt very quickly. Already we talk to a computer that can answer nearly any question, and nobody thinks that's remarkable anymore. So maybe the feeling of normalcy will keep up in some way. But the underlying reality will be very, very different. I think that's the thing to keep in mind.

opus-5.5.text:
You know, one of the things I find quite remarkable is how normal it all feels. If you had told someone a while ago that we'd have these systems, and that companies would be investing amounts on the order of a percent of GDP into AI, they would have imagined it would feel very dramatic. But it doesn't. People get used to things very quickly. You read about it in the news, a company announced some enormous number, and then you go about your day. It's abstract. It doesn't touch you directly yet.

Part of the reason is that there's a real gap between how impressive the models look on evaluations and how much economic impact they actually have so far. That gap is real, and I think it's one of the more confusing things about the current moment.

But I don't think it will stay this way. Once AI genuinely diffuses through the economy, once these systems can actually learn and do real work, I think the impact will be felt very strongly. There will be very powerful economic forces at play, and it will become harder and harder to ignore. I'd also say that it's very hard to feel something that doesn't exist yet. Even people working in the field have trouble imagining what it's like when AI is truly powerful. As the AI becomes more visibly powerful, I expect people's behavior to change, and their sense of how normal things are to change along with it. So the feeling that little has changed is, I think, a feature of where we are right now, not something that will hold all the way through.

r001.rationale: The response connects the sense that little feels different to news of companies announcing enormous AI investment amounts, which people find abstract and then move on from.

r002.rationale: It says that once AI diffuses through the economy, very powerful economic forces will make its impact harder to ignore.

fable-5.text:
I think you have to distinguish between two different things. There is the psychological adaptation, and there is the actual material change in the world, and they behave very differently.

On the psychological side, people are extremely good at normalizing. You see it already. Something that would have seemed like magic five years ago — you talk to a computer and it writes code for you, it explains things to you — within a few weeks of using it, it becomes mundane. It's just how things are. So in that sense, I expect this feeling of "nothing has changed" to persist for longer than you might think, because each increment gets absorbed. The human mind adjusts and makes it the new baseline.

But the material change is a different matter. Right now, there is this strange disconnect where the AI is very impressive when you interact with it, and yet the economic impact, the impact on daily life, is smaller than the capability would suggest. The AI is somehow not fully diffused into the world. I think that gap will close, and when it closes, the change stops being deniable. When AI is actually doing economically meaningful work at scale — when it affects whether you have a job, what medicine you receive, how fast things around you are being built — that is not something that can feel like nothing. You can normalize a chatbot. You cannot normalize the world physically transforming around you.

So my answer would be: the feeling of continuity will last surprisingly long, and then it won't. The singularity, if it deserves the name, is precisely the point where adaptation can no longer keep pace with the change. By definition, that cannot feel like little has changed.

r002.rationale: The response predicts AI’s impact will spread into the economy, but does not attribute that diffusion to strong economic forces.

opus-5.text:
I think there are two things going on, and they pull in opposite directions.

The first is that people adapt really fast. If you'd shown someone in 2013 what we have now — a thing you talk to that writes code, explains your medical test results, does your homework — they'd say the world has been transformed. And in some sense it has. But the way it actually feels from the inside is that you have a new tool, you get used to it in about a week, and then it's just part of the furniture. The baseline moves and your sense of amazement moves with it. So I expect that to continue. Whatever happens, the day-to-day texture of life will feel pretty normal, because the normal is defined by whatever you did yesterday.

But then the second thing is that economic impact is not a feeling. Right now the gap between how good these models look on evals and how much they've actually changed GDP is really strange — much stranger than people acknowledge. I think it's a real signal about something missing, not just a diffusion lag. Models are somehow simultaneously amazing and also unable to be reliably dropped into a job and left alone. But when that gets fixed — and I do think it gets fixed — you're going to have something that isn't like a better tool. If you have a system that can do any job, including the job of improving itself, and it can be copied, then the thing that happens is not "little has changed." The thing that happens is that the entire structure of how anything gets produced changes, and that's not something you can normalize in a week.

So my honest answer is: it will probably feel gradual right up until it doesn't. The subjective experience will be smooth, because it always is, and then at some point you'll look at the world and the smoothness will have delivered you somewhere completely unrecognizable. I don't think people will be walking around saying "wow, the singularity." I think they'll be dealing with very concrete, very large problems — what their work is for, what their government is doing, who controls these systems — and those won't feel like science fiction. They'll feel like politics.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's a bit of a mixed picture. Right now there's something very strange going on. You read that companies are announcing investments of hundreds of billions of dollars, and it all feels abstract, like something that only exists in the news. Then you walk outside and nothing seems different. I think that feeling will stick around for a while, because so far the progress hasn't shown up in everyday life in a way people can point to.

But I don't think it lasts all the way through. The feeling that little has changed comes from the fact that the economic impact hasn't spread yet. Once AI really diffuses through the economy, I expect the effect to be very strong and very hard to miss, and that will be a different kind of moment. The difficulty is that I don't know exactly when it happens, and I suspect it won't arrive all at once. Some places will feel it enormously and others much later.

So in the near term, yes, I think a lot of people will keep feeling that it's just another headline. Past a certain point, though, I don't think "nothing has changed" will remain a believable description. If you actually have systems that can learn and do the work of people, the world can't stay the same.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think there's a real possibility that for a while, a lot of people's day-to-day lives won't look that different, even as the underlying technology gets dramatically more capable. Technologies usually take time to show up in how people actually live, because organizations have to adopt them, workflows have to be rebuilt around them, and trust has to be earned. So the gap between what's possible in a lab and what someone experiences on a Tuesday afternoon can be wide.

But I don't think that gap lasts forever. Once systems can do most of the cognitive work that people do, and do it reliably, I'd expect the change to become very visible very quickly. It might not feel like a gradual drift. It might feel like the ground moving under a lot of institutions at once.

So my honest answer is: the stability people feel now is probably real, but I wouldn't read too much into it. The question I'd be watching is less "does my life look different yet" and more "are the things that determine how the world runs starting to be done by systems that aren't human."

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it depends on what you mean by “little has changed.” You could have very dramatic progress in AI, and for some period your day still looks quite similar. You wake up, you have breakfast, you see your friends. Those things can continue.

But if we’re talking about superintelligence, something that can do everything that we can do and much more, then I don’t think the consequences can remain confined to your computer. Eventually they have to affect the world you live in.

The harder question is how long that takes. The capabilities could change very quickly, while their consequences take longer to become apparent.

I don’t think so. I think there can be a delay between having a very powerful technology and feeling its effects in your daily life. You still wake up, you have breakfast, you go to work. And you can point to that and say, well, things seem pretty normal.

But if we’re talking about AI that can do everything that people can do, then at some point that normality has to change. The work people do, the things we can discover, the decisions we have to make. I’m much less sure about how quickly that happens. But I don’t think you can have something that transformative and have the average person’s life remain unchanged indefinitely.
